clinicalPearls: A periapical abscess is a localised collection of pus at the root apex arising from a necrotic, infected pulp
Classic features are severe, well-localised pain, tenderness to percussion, and a feeling that the tooth is extruded or high on biting
The affected tooth is typically non-vital, so pulp sensibility testing is negative while percussion and palpation are markedly positive
Pus may drain spontaneously through a sinus tract (gum boil), which can relieve pain and produce a chronic, less symptomatic picture
Early radiographs may look normal because bone changes lag behind, whereas chronic lesions show a periapical radiolucency
Primary management is drainage and elimination of the source through root canal treatment or extraction; antibiotics are adjuncts reserved for spreading infection or systemic involvement
Infection can track along fascial planes, so the pattern of swelling depends on tooth position relative to muscle attachments
Recurrent or persistent sinus tracts indicate ongoing infection needing definitive endodontic or surgical treatment
reference.pathophysiology: A periapical abscess develops when pulp necrosis, usually secondary to caries or trauma, allows bacteria and their toxins to egress through the apical foramen into the periapical tissues. The host inflammatory response produces a purulent collection localised to the periradicular bone. Rising pressure causes intense pain and may resorb surrounding bone, seen later as a radiolucency. Pus follows the path of least resistance, perforating cortical bone and tracking into soft tissue, where the relationship of the perforation to muscle attachments determines whether a localised vestibular swelling, a draining sinus, or a spreading fascial-space infection results.
additionalDifferentials: Periodontal abscess arising from the gingival sulcus
Odontogenic infection of adjacent teeth or sinus
additionalInvestigations: Periapical radiography and, when needed, cone-beam CT for extent
Assessment for fascial-space spread and airway compromise in swelling
Culture and systemic markers if severe or spreading infection
redFlags: Rapidly spreading swelling of the floor of mouth or submandibular region raising concern for Ludwig angina and airway obstruction
Trismus, difficulty swallowing, drooling, or voice change indicating deep-space infection
Systemic sepsis, high fever, or periorbital/cavernous sinus spread from upper anterior teeth
Immunocompromised or diabetic patients in whom infection can progress dangerously fast
reference.prognosis: With timely drainage and source control the prognosis is excellent, but delayed treatment risks spread to fascial spaces, osteomyelitis, airway compromise, or life-threatening sepsis.
pitfalls: Prescribing antibiotics without draining the abscess or removing the source
Being reassured by a normal early radiograph despite clear clinical signs
Missing progression to a deep-space or airway-threatening infection
Confusing a periodontal abscess with a periapical abscess and mistreating the cause
